title: False Memory and Source Monitoring
summary: The learner studies three original themed lists of eight items, each item labelled with one of two named sources, and is then tested on twelve words: six studied, three related words that were never presented, and three unrelated words that were never presented. Recognition, confidence and source attribution are collected as three separate judgements and reported as three separate measures, because the places where they come apart are the finding. A transfer challenge asks what changing source distinctiveness, delay, forewarning and list length would do to each measure.
learningObjectives: Separate recognition, confidence and source attribution as three measures that can diverge.
Explain a gist-based intrusion without claiming that memory is unreliable.
Describe source monitoring as an inference made at retrieval rather than a stored label.
Use an unrelated-new baseline to interpret an endorsement rate.
Predict how source distinctiveness, delay, warning and list length affect each measure differently.
interactionTypes: recognition and confidence in a single judgement
unrelated-new baseline as a bias check
bar chart paired with a data table
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; study and test responses stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage. The record of which themes have been used is a JavaScript variable that survives a reset within the tab and disappears on reload.
accessibilityNotes: The study card changes once every 1.5 to 3 seconds at the learner's chosen pace and only its contents change; the card, its size and its position stay put. The test phase is not timed at all, and no CSS animation or transition is used anywhere, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. The two sources are distinguished by their full name printed above every studied word and by a solid or dashed left rule - never by hue. Response buttons state their answer in words including the confidence level, carry an explicit accessible name naming the word being judged, and are at least 3rem tall. The stage track marks the current phase with a border, a background and aria-current=step as well as a number. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a five-column table; each bar prints its own percentage and mean confidence, and the related-word bar is hatched as well as differently filled. The study card is aria-hidden while presenting. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading and to the first option of each question, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the card, the test word and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
readmeTopic: False memory and source monitoring: recognition, confidence and source can disagree
simulationNotes: All word lists are original to this tool: six themes of eight items each, with a critical lure per theme that is never presented. No published word list is reproduced. A run uses three themes not yet spent, so the demonstration can be run fresh exactly twice; the tool tracks and reports how many fresh themes remain, and that record deliberately survives a reset because a theme a learner has already studied is no longer fresh material. Within each theme, four items come from each source, so source is not confounded with theme, and themes are presented blocked. The test set is six studied items (two per theme), three critical lures and three unrelated words, shuffled. Recognition and confidence are collected in a single click (not seen / seen and guessing / seen and fairly sure / seen and certain) and source is asked only of endorsed items, with an explicit I-cannot-tell option. The unrelated-new row is the response-bias check and the limits panel says that the raw rates are not corrected for bias. The worked example is a simulated class of 60 fictional participants with mulberry32 seed 20261001: endorsement .84 for studied items, .61 for lures and .09 for unrelated items; confidence given endorsement distributed with certain at .62 / .38 / .08 and fairly-sure thresholds at .92 / .80 / .35; source correct on .71 of placed studied items; and 72 per cent of endorsed lures and unrelated items given a source they never had. It produces 85 per cent, 61 per cent and 11 per cent endorsement with mean confidences of 2.5, 2.2 and 1.4 out of 3, and 70 per cent source accuracy on studied items. That pattern is built in to illustrate the classic finding; it is not evidence for it, not a norm and not anybody's data. The tool deliberately avoids framing any of this as evidence that memory is unreliable.
